summary: An announcement that the weather demonstration built for the ICCC show is generally available. It consists of two programs, a natural language program in LISP and a primitive Datacomputer, which talk over the network to answer English questions about weather.

plainLanguage.summary: The Weather demonstration uses one program to interpret questions and another to retrieve weather records. The programs communicate over the network, but the notice describes limits on the questions and data they can handle.

subtitle: A networked program for asking questions about weather data

tldr.problem: The Weather demonstration needed to interpret a user's English question and retrieve matching weather records.
tldr.mechanism: A LISP program processes the question and communicates over the network with a Datacomputer that stores weather data, using Datalanguage.
tldr.outcome: The RFC makes the demonstration available and explains its operating limits, data and example requests.

today: RFC 420 describes an evolving Weather demonstration and its operating instructions. It states that the system's behavior and the data could change, and lists limitations known at the time.

sections.title: Two Programs Working Together
sections.content:
The demonstration consists of two independent programs. A LISP natural-language program, modified from a system developed by T. Winograd at MIT, handles questions in English. A primitive Datacomputer stores weather information and provides data management facilities. The programs communicate over the network using Datalanguage.

The example question is whether it rained in Boston on a particular date.
sections.plainLanguage: One program works out what a question asks. The other looks up weather records, and the two exchange requests over the network.

sections.title: Asking a Weather Question
sections.content:
After starting Weather, the user enters a Julian date for the current day and then types a sentence ending with punctuation. The system tries to identify the words and correct spelling as input arrives. It may treat an unknown word as a possible place name, and an equals sign can mark a city name as a proper noun.

The RFC includes an example in which the system checks a city name and then requests weather observations from the Datacomputer.
sections.plainLanguage: The user enters a date and types a question about the weather. Weather turns the question into data requests and returns an answer when it can.

sections.title: Limits of the Language System
sections.content:
The authors warn that the system is not linguistically sophisticated. It works best with simple requests for weather information and does not truly understand weather; it composes requests to retrieve records from its database. The RFC lists conjunction, negation, complex quantification, sophisticated pronoun reference and questions unrelated to weather as known limitations.

The notice says an answer takes about a minute on average and describes the data as incomplete or summarized in some respects.
sections.plainLanguage: The program handles simple weather questions, not general conversation. It may fail on complex sentences, and the data described in the notice has gaps.

sections.title: Running the Demonstration
sections.content: The RFC says the LISP program uses CPU and core resources, so users are asked to prefer running it on their own machine and to check with CCA staff before using CCA's machine. The Datacomputer is described as less demanding, but only one user at a time could run it then. The notice gives operating and maintenance guidance and points users to files containing current information.
sections.plainLanguage: The LISP program uses substantial computer resources. The Datacomputer had a one-user limit, and the notice asks users to avoid busy periods and check current instructions.
